fields.Front: First law of thermodynamics (PHYS 221 sign convention)
fields.Back: \(\delta Q=dU+\delta W\), with \(Q>0\) for heat into the system and \(W>0\) for work done by it
fields.SpeakFront: the first law of thermodynamics, in the PHYS 221 sign convention
fields.SpeakBack: delta Q equals d U plus delta W; heat into the system is positive, and work done by the system is positive
fields.Elaboration: Chemistry often writes \(\Delta U=Q+W\) with \(W\) done on the system. Same physics, opposite sign for \(W\).

golden.note: The sign convention sits in the prompt (canon 2). The chemistry convention in Elaboration guards against interference from CHEM 107 cards.

fields.Back: \(Q\) and \(W\) depend on the path (inexact differentials); \(U\) is a state function (exact)
fields.Elaboration: Different paths between the same two states enclose different \(pV\) areas: \(W\) differs, \(\Delta U\) doesn't.
fields.Front: Why are heat and work written \(\delta Q,\ \delta W\) but internal energy \(dU\)?
fields.SpeakBack: heat and work depend on the path, so their differentials are inexact; internal energy is a state function, so d U is exact
fields.SpeakFront: why are heat and work written with a small delta, but internal energy with d?

golden.note: Revision: trimmed.

fields.Front: Work done by a gas during a volume change
fields.Back: \(W=\displaystyle\int_{V_1}^{V_2}p\,dV\): the area under the path on a pV diagram
fields.SpeakFront: work done by a gas during a volume change
fields.SpeakBack: the integral of p d V from V one to V two; the area under the path on a p V diagram
fields.Elaboration: From \(dW=F\,dx=pA\,dx=p\,dV\). Compression gives negative work.

golden.note: The F → p step in Elaboration answers the red 'how get F → p?'.

fields.Front: Internal energy of an ideal gas depends on which state variable?
fields.SpeakBack: temperature only
fields.SpeakFront: internal energy of an ideal gas depends on which state variable?

golden.note: Revision: true for every ideal gas, not just monatomic, so it stands alone.

fields.Situation: Finding \(\Delta U\) of an ideal gas in a process that isn't at constant volume
fields.Trap: Thinking \(\Delta U=nC_V\Delta T\) only holds for isochoric processes
fields.Fix: For an ideal gas, \(\Delta U=nC_V\Delta T\) for any process
fields.Why: \(U\) depends on \(T\) alone. \(C_V\) is just the constant-volume way of measuring \(dU/dT\).
fields.SpeakSituation: finding the change in internal energy of an ideal gas in a process that is not at constant volume
fields.SpeakFix: for an ideal gas, delta U equals n C V delta T for any process

golden.note: Answers the red 'always true?' on Exam Example 32.

fields.Front: Specific heat \(c\) vs molar heat capacity \(C\): what does each count per?
fields.Back: \(c\): per kilogram (\(\delta Q=cm\Delta T\)). \(C\): per mole (\(\delta Q=Cn\Delta T\)).
fields.SpeakFront: specific heat, small c, versus molar heat capacity, capital C; what does each count per?
fields.SpeakBack: small c is per kilogram, with mass m; capital C is per mole, with n moles
fields.Elaboration: \(n=m/M\), where \(M\) is the molar mass. Watch which one a problem gives you.

golden.note: The red 'n vs m?' appears twice, so it gets a contrast card whose prompt asks for the contrast (canon 1).

fields.Front: Molar heat capacity \(C_V\) of a monatomic ideal gas
fields.SpeakFront: molar heat capacity at constant volume, C V, of a monatomic ideal gas
fields.SpeakBack: three halves R
fields.Elaboration: From \(U=\tfrac32nRT\): \(dU/dT\) per mole. About 12.5 J/(mol·K) (He, Ar).

golden.note: Numeric Elaboration, checked: 1.5 × 8.314 = 12.47.

fields.Elaboration: Real polyatomic gases deviate a little (CO₂: 8.48 vs 8.31 J/(mol·K)).
fields.Front: \(C_P-C_V\) for an ideal gas (molar heat capacities)
fields.SpeakBack: R
fields.SpeakFront: C P minus C V for an ideal gas, molar heat capacities

golden.note: Revision: the value, split from the why.

fields.Back: At constant pressure, part of the heat goes into expansion work, so more heat is needed per degree
fields.Elaboration: The extra is \(p\,\Delta V=nR\,\Delta T\) per \(\Delta T\), which is where \(C_P-C_V=R\) comes from.
fields.Front: Why is \(C_P>C_V\) for an ideal gas?
fields.SpeakBack: at constant pressure part of the heat goes into expansion work, so more heat is needed per degree
fields.SpeakFront: why is C P greater than C V for an ideal gas?

golden.note: Revision: the why, as its own card.

fields.Front: Adiabatic index \(\gamma=C_P/C_V\): monatomic vs diatomic ideal gas
fields.SpeakFront: the adiabatic index gamma, C P over C V, for a monatomic versus a diatomic ideal gas
fields.SpeakBack: five thirds for monatomic, seven fifths for diatomic, with rotation active and vibration frozen out
fields.Elaboration: More degrees of freedom raise \(C_V\), and \(\gamma\) moves toward 1. A higher \(\gamma\) means a steeper adiabat.

golden.note: A contrast card, since the contrast is the point. Elaboration answers 'what does higher γ mean?'.

fields.Front: Work done by \(n\) mol of ideal gas in an isothermal change \(V_i\to V_f\)
fields.SpeakFront: work done by n moles of ideal gas in an isothermal change from V i to V f
fields.SpeakBack: n R T times the natural log of V f over V i; and since delta U is zero, the heat equals the work
fields.Elaboration: Integrate \(p=nRT/V\). \(W\ne p\Delta V\) because \(p\) varies along the path.

golden.note: Answers the red 'W = pΔV? what do you need to integrate?'.

review.reason: W neq p delta v should be its own card w/ why

fields.Back: The pressure changes along the path (\(p=nRT/V\)), so you have to integrate: \(W=\int p\,dV\)
fields.Elaboration: \(W=p\,\Delta V\) only holds when \(p\) is constant (isobaric).
fields.Front: Why isn't the work in an isothermal ideal-gas expansion \(p\,\Delta V\)?
fields.SpeakBack: because the pressure changes along the path, so you have to integrate p d V
fields.SpeakFront: why isn't the work in an isothermal ideal gas expansion p delta V?

golden.note: Your review: W ≠ pΔV gets its own card, with the why.

fields.Front: Adiabatic process for an ideal gas: the p–V relation
fields.SpeakFront: adiabatic process for an ideal gas, the p V relation
fields.SpeakBack: p V to the gamma is constant; equivalently T V to the gamma minus one is constant
fields.Elaboration: Adiabatic means \(Q=0\): no heat exchange, e.g. a thermally insulated system or a process too fast for heat to flow.

golden.note: The meaning of 'adiabatic' goes in Elaboration, answering 'isothermal vs adiabatic?'.

fields.Front: Why is an adiabat steeper than an isotherm on a pV diagram?
fields.Back: Expanding adiabatically, the gas pays for its work out of \(U\), so \(T\) drops as well and \(p\) falls faster: \(p\propto V^{-\gamma}\) vs \(V^{-1}\), with \(\gamma>1\)
fields.SpeakFront: why is an adiabat steeper than an isotherm on a p V diagram?
fields.SpeakBack: because the gas pays for its work out of internal energy, so the temperature drops too and the pressure falls faster; p goes as V to the minus gamma instead of V to the minus one
fields.Elaboration: Isothermal: heat flows in to hold \(T\), so \(p\) falls only through \(V\).

golden.note: The student's guess ('more internal energy lost?') was right; the card makes it precise.

fields.Front: Work done by an ideal gas in an adiabatic process
fields.SpeakFront: work done by an ideal gas in an adiabatic process
fields.SpeakBack: minus delta U, which is n C V times T i minus T f, which also equals p i V i minus p f V f, over gamma minus one
fields.Elaboration: \(Q=0\), so the first law gives \(W=-\Delta U\). Positive work means the gas cools.

fields.Front: Exam Example 26 result: \(C_p-C_V\) for a general (nonideal) gas
fields.Elaboration: Key move: write \(dU(T,V(T,p))\) with the chain rule at constant \(p\). For an ideal gas, \((\partial U/\partial V)_T=0\) and \(p(\partial V/\partial T)_p=R\), giving \(R\).

fields.Front: Exam Example 27, key step: from \(\delta Q=0\) to \(pV^\gamma=\text{const}\)
fields.Back: \(nC_V\,dT=-p\,dV\) with \(p=nRT/V\) gives \(\dfrac{dT}{T}=-(\gamma-1)\dfrac{dV}{V}\). Integrate to get \(TV^{\gamma-1}=\text{const}\), then substitute \(T=pV/nR\).
fields.SpeakFront: Exam example 27, the key step from zero heat to p V to the gamma constant
fields.SpeakBack: set n C V d T equal to minus p d V with p equal to n R T over V, which gives d T over T equals minus gamma minus one, times d V over V; integrate, then substitute T equals p V over n R
fields.Elaboration: Uses \(R/C_V=(C_P-C_V)/C_V=\gamma-1\).

golden.note: Exam-labelled derivation: card the key move, not the whole derivation (principle 6: support derivation, don't replace it).
